Header:

Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Gupta (Redwood SRE); Carlos Mendez (Streamline ML Eng), Rina Sharma (Infra Lead), Jessie Lee (CTO)

Summary: Focused on profiling GPU runtime for large models, kernel selection and heuristics, comparing TensorRT-LLM and v-LLM paths, using CUDA graphs to reduce launch overhead, and how KV cache interacts with batching and long-running chat sessions.

00:00 Alex Chen: hey everyone, um thanks for joining. we wanted to get into the kernel-level profiling you sent and talk through tradeoffs between t-rt l-l-m and v-llm, plus some notes on cuda graphs.
00:18 Carlos Mendez: great, yeah thanks, our main pain is tail latency spikes under mixed workloads and then when we enable persistent sessions KV cache behaves kinda weird, we see memory thrashing.
00:34 Priya Patel: ok yeah. quick context: we looked at your traces you uploaded to the share link, there were a couple things - kernel selection toggles, and we noticed repeated small kernel launches during attention for long context.
00:52 Rina Sharma: sorry one sec, are we talking about our prod traces or the synthetic that we ran? the prod traces are on the S3 bucket, link in the doc.
01:05 Priya Patel: both - Carlos uploaded the prod set and also the synthetic. prod shows a lot of small seq lengths but with occasional long-prefix sessions which kills throughput.
01:22 Samir Gupta: just to add, we saw a big CPU-GPU sync on the first token after a fallback to a CPU-based kernel - that correlates with your 98th percentile latency spike.
01:38 Carlos Mendez: hmm that sounds right, we saw some fallbacks but i'm not sure if it's from quantization or an unsupported op path.
01:47 Priya Patel: likely kernel mismatch for rotary embeddings or an einsum pattern. t-rt llm's auto-kernel chooser will often pick a TensorRT fused kernel which is fast but has strict shapes - when a request deviates it falls back to a more general kernel or runtime interpreter, that triggers the sync.
02:07 Jessie Lee: and v-llm? How does v-llm handle that? our bench person mentioned v-llm had better steady-state throughput for our sequences.
02:17 Priya Patel: v-llm tends to use optimized CUDA kernels but can be more conservative on fusions; it's great for batching and dynamic shapes, but TensorRT-LLM can beat it when inputs fit the fused kernel shapes and you use CUDA graphs to eliminate launch overhead. it's a tradeoff - t-rt llm wins on P50/P75 when shapes are stable, v-llm sometimes better P95 for variable shapes.
02:44 Carlos Mendez: ok that aligns. what about CUDA graphs? we tried enabling them but didn't see the improvement we expected.
02:51 Priya Patel: common. two things: one, warmup - you need a few warm invocations to capture the graph with representative inputs. two, if your input shapes vary a lot, graphs can get invalidated and rebuilt, which costs. in your traces we saw frequent graph re-captures every ~30s in one session.
03:10 Rina Sharma: is that from our front-end sending variable tokenization lengths?
03:15 Priya Patel: yes, variable padding and tokenization length can cause it. we recommend bucketing sequences and/or using logical batching to keep representative shapes. also capturing graphs for a set of canonical lengths (e.g., 32, 128, 512) reduces rebuilds.
03:32 Carlos Mendez: ok, tell me more about the KV cache interplay - our memory blows up and then the scheduler starts evicting things and latency spikes again.
03:40 Priya Patel: KV cache memory is linear with sequence length and number of concurrent sessions. We saw in your logs sessions with 40k tokens retained - that alone will exhaust a single A100's 80GB if you have many concurrent users. Redwood runtime supports sharded KV across GPUs and prefix caching to reduce duplication, but on single-GPU setups you need to evict intelligently or quantize KV to lower precision.
04:05 Samir Gupta: we also noticed kernel sizes changed when using 8-bit quant; some fused kernels aren't supported in INT8 so the runtime falls back. that's another source of sync.
04:17 Priya Patel: right, quantization often introduces kernel compatibility issues. Our quantization recommendation: use QAT for sensitive ops or hybrid kernels where matmuls run in INT8 but attention uses FP16, that keeps fused kernels available.
04:33 Jessie Lee: can you share an example profile showing the fallback path?
04:38 Priya Patel: yes, i'll upload the nvprof and nsight timelines. in the trace you shared the sequence was: fused attention kernel -> small-shape mismatch -> python op fallback -> cpu postprocessing -> cuda sync. that sequence eats ~120ms on that request.
04:58 Carlos Mendez: ouch.
05:01 Alex Chen: to add, one lever we use is shape-aware batching: group requests by len and run per-bucket graphs. that keeps graph stability and high GPU utilization. i'll include that.
05:18 Rina Sharma: what about kernel selector heuristics? is that a runtime knob?
05:23 Priya Patel: yes, runtime exposes kernel selection policies: optimize_for_latency, optimize_for_throughput, and a hybrid. For throughput you allow larger batch sizes and more aggressive fusion; latency mode keeps batch sizes smaller and prefers low-p99. We saw your config set to throughput default, which explains the P95 spikes for single-user sessions.
05:42 Carlos Mendez: ah we didn't realize that. can you show how to toggle it?
05:46 Priya Patel: sure, small demo later; config flag is model.runtime.kernel_policy = hybrid (or latency/throughput). We'll send sample config.
05:55 Alex Chen: switching gears - we compared TensorRT-LLM and vLLM on a 2k-context Llama-2-70B-ish workload. t-rt had 20% lower per-token latency when shapes were bucketed and graphs pre-captured; v-llm had more graceful degradation with highly variable shape mixes.
06:15 Carlos Mendez: interesting. do you have numbers? we can reproduce.
06:20 Priya Patel: yes, i'll push the benchmark sheet link to the doc - it has p50/p95 and token/sec. i'll also include kernel-level breakdowns.
06:30 Rina Sharma: curious re: CUDA graphs - do they play nicely with multi-GPU sharded KV?
06:36 Priya Patel: they do, but capture needs to be coordinated across GPUs. the graph capture must reflect the sharded memory pointers. Redwood runtime handles coordinated capture, but you need a stable placement mapping during capture. for autoscaling clusters it gets trickier.
06:54 Samir Gupta: note for on-prem / VPC: if you're using our Private deployment, we recommend pinning GPU placement during initial warmups and then enabling autoscale only after warm graphs are stabilized.
07:08 Jessie Lee: and networking? we saw some latency added by VPC ENI attachment when scaling up.
07:13 Priya Patel: yep, network path and node startup are separate concerns - cold-starts for dedicated nodes cause graph invalidation and a transient hit. that's why we recommend a small warm pool for low-latency SLAs.
07:26 Carlos Mendez: ok makes sense. another question: CUDA graph memory - is it persistent? we've seen memory fragmentation over time.
07:33 Priya Patel: captured graphs hold some persistent device allocations; fragmentation can increase if you capture many graphs with slightly different shapes. consolidating to canonical buckets reduces fragmentation. periodic restarts in maintenance windows help too.
07:50 Rina Sharma: about quantization: you mentioned hybrid kernels. how invasive is switching to hybrid for our stack?
07:56 Priya Patel: minimal code changes - mostly config and per-op casting. We'll help with a small POC: run 8-bit matmuls, keep attention in FP16, validate quality with eval prompts. In our experience quality regression is often <1% on perplexity for chat usecases if you tune well.
08:18 Carlos Mendez: great. regarding the profiler artifacts, what's the best way to share them? we already put nvprof, Nsight, and a small flamegraph in S3.
08:26 Alex Chen: perfect - please also include the raw per-kernel timing CSV (we referenced it in the doc). We'll ingest it into our profiler to generate per-model recommendations.
08:36 Priya Patel: and please include the request sampler JSON so we can replay on our infra. that helps reproduce the graph rebuild pattern.
08:44 Carlos Mendez: will do.

12:15 Priya Patel: walkthrough of a captured timeline: in this example we see a 3-phase pattern - capture, stable serving, rebuild. the rebuild correlates with a sudden token length > captured max, causing a graph recapture which spikes latency for that request and subsequent ones until it finishes.
12:40 Rina Sharma: is there an automated way to detect and fallback gracefully?
12:46 Priya Patel: yes, runtime can detect high rebuild frequency and fall back to a permissive kernel mode until you re-capture with a better canonical set. we can toggle that threshold.
13:00 Carlos Mendez: about multi-tenancy, how do you avoid noisy neighbor for KV cache heavy sessions?
13:06 Samir Gupta: we recommend per-customer KV shard quotas and a cap on retained tokens per session; plus evictor policies based on recency and utility score. we can surface token retention metrics in the console.
13:20 Jessie Lee: excellent. can we get a sample config for eviction thresholds?
13:24 Alex Chen: yes, i'll attach a sample in the follow-up.
13:28 Rina Sharma: any gotchas for on-prem with custom NICs? we run Mellanox HDR.
13:33 Priya Patel: RDMA is great for sharded KV performance but you need correct CUDA-aware MPI stacks; some kernel captures fail if endpoints aren't CUDA-aware. our Private deployment checklist includes NIC driver versions and IB configs.
13:50 Carlos Mendez: that may be our issue, we didn't enable CUDA-aware verbs.
13:54 Priya Patel: check the driver and libibverbs versions; we'll send the checklist.
